From the end of the Kamakura period, longer and heavier swords came into fashion, and the fashion carried on into the next age. When the Warring States brought mass tactics with spears and guns, the craze cooled. Cooled, I say, not died: among warriors it never fully went away.

Consider Juurouzaemon Magara, a mighty general in Asakura service, said to have swung a great sword of seven shaku three sun. Over seven feet. That is not a weapon, that is a lamp-post with a bad temper.

Why did the fashion begin? Theories are many; certainty is nil. One theory blames the Mongol invasions. The Yamato warriors had burnt their hands on hard Mongol steel, so they demanded a blade strong enough to break it. Logic of the simplest kind: wall is hard, hammer must be big.

But a great sword without the strength to wield it is only luggage. And circumstances bind it also.

Ground, especially ground with many obstacles, does not suit it. By the theory, the book answer, Ichijou should now take to the air. But—

Kageaki Minato was leaning against a tree.

It was plain he had no strength left to stand. Cut up like that, no one could move.

His wounds were making a gritty, grinding sound.

They were burning. In heat that had not yet cooled.

A similar sound came from my own right arm. The hand holding my sword was burning too.

There was no pain. Probably the nerves had already burned through.

Arm and sword were welded into a single rod. Still, I could move it.

This tsurugi would grant strength to me for as long as I wished to fight.

I walked up to the crimson warrior. The blade, smoking as it burned off every raindrop, I put to his throat.
